reason: The dominant stabilizing feature is the five-membered intramolecular O-H...N contact of this beta-amino alcohol. Conformer 8 has an H...N distance of about 2.22 A, favorable approach toward the nitrogen lone-pair side, an approximately anti terminal alkyl torsion, and the oxygen anti to the propyl-side carbon; it therefore has the best overall balance. Conformer 30 has similarly good hydrogen-bond and lone-pair alignment but pays a terminal-chain gauche penalty. Conformer 5 has an anti terminal chain and a good H...N contact near 2.27 A, although oxygen is gauche to the propyl-side carbon, while 22 has a comparably good hydrogen bond but a somewhat less favorable substituent arrangement about the central C-C bond. Conformers 17, 23, 15, and 20 retain clear H...N contacts near 2.2-2.3 A but contain, respectively, extra central or terminal gauche interactions; 20 has both. Conformers 21 and 12 also hydrogen bond, but their central torsions are noticeably displaced from ideal staggered values. Conformers 4, 19, and 27 have useful O-H...N contacts, yet their terminal C-C-C-C torsions are around the roughly 90-105 degree region rather than anti or normal gauche; this introduces appreciable torsional/eclipsing strain. The especially short H...N distance in 19 does not fully compensate for that strain and for having both larger central substituents gauche to the chain. Conformer 13 has a weaker H...N contact near 2.36 A together with terminal gauche and distorted central torsions. Conformer 25 is fully extended in the alkyl portion and has O and N close, but its H...N distance near 2.54 A and poor O-H...N direction make the hydrogen bond weak. Conformer 29 is the best non-hydrogen-bonded extended geometry: the terminal chain is anti and the aziridinyl substituent is placed anti to the propyl group, but O and N are far apart. Conformers 26 and 2 are similarly extended but use the alternative central staggered rotamer. Conformer 16 has a favorable extended chain but only a marginal, poorly directed H...N approach near 2.6 A. Conformers 14 and 24 lack hydrogen bonding and place both larger central substituents gauche to the propyl chain. Conformers 1 and 6 have weak, poorly directed donor-acceptor approaches and terminal gauche chains; 9 is non-hydrogen-bonded but reasonably staggered. Conformers 7 and 11 combine weak donor-acceptor geometry with less favorable central or terminal gauche arrangements. Conformer 18 lacks hydrogen bonding and has a significantly nonideal central torsion. Conformers 10 and 28 have terminal gauche chains and unfavorable central placement, with 28 additionally bringing O and N together without productive O-H...N alignment. Conformer 3 combines a terminal gauche chain, a distorted central torsion, and only a very weak H...N approach, making it the least favorable estimate. Aziridine bond lengths and ring geometry are similar throughout, so differential ring strain is small. The closest calls are 30 versus 5, 17 versus 23, 21 versus 12, 25 versus 29, and the 2/26 and 14/24 pairs; their order could change with a quantitative electronic-structure calculation.

The molecule is acyclic, and all conformers retain normal local bond lengths and a nearly planar carboxamide, so the ranking is governed mainly by torsional strain, weak intramolecular hydrogen bonds, carbonyl–nitrile dipole alignment, and folding of the ethyl group. Conformer 22 has the best combined geometry: an N–H···O contact of about 2.20 Å with an approximately 111° angle, nearly antiparallel carbonyl and nitrile bond vectors (about 151°), and an extended ethyl arrangement. Conformers 19 and 5 have similarly favorable N–H···O contacts (about 2.17 and 2.15 Å, approximately 113°) and carbonyl/nitrile angles near 146°, but their ethyl groups are more gauche, placing the terminal and central carbons only about 3.15 and 3.07 Å apart. Conformers 13 and 14 instead form six-membered amide-N–H···N≡C arrangements: H···N is about 2.72 Å with angles near 123°, while the carbonyl and nitrile dipoles are strongly opposed (about 149–150°). The extended ethyl geometry in 13 makes it substantially better than the gauche geometry in 14; 13 is therefore competitive with the strongest N–H···O structures. Conformer 8 also combines favorable dipole opposition with a 2.30 Å N–H···O contact, although it is folded. Conformers 17, 6, and 2 retain favorable carbonyl/nitrile opposition and relatively open geometries, but their hydrogen bonds are longer or poorly angled. In the middle group, 10 and 30 have short N–H···O contacts but less favorable carbonyl/nitrile alignment, while 27, 9, and 12 have short amide-N–H···amine-N contacts (roughly 2.11–2.16 Å and 107–110°) but comparatively aligned or near-perpendicular carbonyl and nitrile dipoles. Conformers 20, 1, 4, 7, 23, and 18 represent compromises between weaker contacts, dipole alignment, and ethyl extension. Conformers 25, 26, 28, and 11 retain geometrically plausible amide-N–H···amine-N contacts, but combine them with folded ethyl groups and unfavorable carbonyl/nitrile orientations. Conformers 21, 24, 16, 29, and especially 15 lack a comparably effective hydrogen bond or antiparallel dipole arrangement; 15 is both folded and has only a long, poorly directed heteroatom contact. There are no severe atomic overlaps, so differences within the middle and lower groups are subtle and their detailed order is uncertain; the most robust distinctions are the favorable folded-contact/dipole combinations at the top and the absence of those features at the bottom.

The molecule is acyclic, so there is no ring strain; all structures also have normal bonding distances and no catastrophic nonbonded clash. The dominant distinction is the O=C-Cα-N torsion. Conformers 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 12, 13, 17, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, and 30 place the carbonyl and C-N bond directions broadly antiparallel: N is about 3.4-3.6 A from the carbonyl oxygen, reducing O/N electrostatic repulsion and cancelling the carbonyl and amine bond dipoles. The remaining conformers place N only about 2.78 A from the carbonyl oxygen and have much more parallel local dipoles, so they are assigned lower stability. A second important coordinate is the terminal-C-C-O-C(=O) torsion. The extended ethyl arrangements have terminal-C to carbonyl-C distances near 3.6 A and avoid folding the terminal methyl over the carbonyl; the gauche arrangements have this distance near 3.1 A and terminal-C to carbonyl-O distances near 3.23 A, introducing mild CH/O crowding. Thus extended, antiparallel-backbone structures form the leading group: 12, 21, 3, 19, 25, 4, and 13 have the most nearly antiparallel C=O/C-N geometry, followed closely by the slightly twisted but still favorable 26 and 24. Their internal ordering is based only on small differences in methyl clearance and weak NH/O contacts. The corresponding gauche-ethyl structures follow: 20, 9, 30, and 23 retain the best backbone alignment; 10, 6, and 27 are slightly more twisted; 22 and 17 have the least antiparallel C=O/C-N geometry of this favorable-backbone set. Among the carbonyl-O/N-close structures, 16, 14, 1, and 7 have extended ethyl groups and a modest torsional displacement that reduces direct dipole alignment, making them preferable to 18, 5, 11, and 29. Gauche ethyl conformers 15 and 8 are then penalized further, while 28 and 2 combine the folded ethyl group with the least favorable carbonyl-O/N-close backbone orientation. Several H...O separations are around 2.35-2.6 A, but the N-H...O angles are generally only about 95-105 degrees, so these are weak electrostatic contacts rather than strong intramolecular hydrogen bonds. Consequently, ordering within each small subfamily is uncertain and likely represents energy differences of only a few tenths of a kcal/mol; the separation between the main torsional families is more reliable.

The connectivity is an acyclic propargyl ether bearing a secondary alcohol, so there is no ring strain; the main energy differences arise from the C3-C4-O-C6 and C4-O-C6-C7 backbone torsions, the O-C-C-O arrangement, and the alcohol orientation. First, conformers 17, 18, 29, and 28 combine an extended C4-O-C6-C7 segment (C4···C7 about 3.68 Å) with an O-C-C-O gauche arrangement (O···O about 2.77 Å), the methyl approximately anti to the ether oxygen, and a weak five-membered O-H···O interaction with H···O about 2.29 Å. They therefore form the most favorable, nearly degenerate group. Conformer 27 has especially favorable anti-like arrangements for both backbone torsions (C3···C6 about 3.61 Å and C4···C7 about 3.68 Å), but around the alcohol-bearing bond the ether oxygen is anti to H rather than methyl; this leaves both OH and methyl gauche to the ether oxygen and gives a slightly poorer O-H···O geometry. Conformers 12, 13, and 5 have the shortest intramolecular H···O contacts, about 2.20-2.21 Å, and methyl-anti O-C-C-C geometry, but their C4-O-C6-C7 torsion is gauche (C4···C7 about 3.1 Å), so they follow the more extended structures. Conformers 23, 20, 1, and 14 retain an extended backbone and place the two oxygens anti, with O···O around 3.6 Å; they avoid O/O crowding but lose the intramolecular hydrogen-bond stabilization. Conformers 24, 21, and 9 also have an extended backbone and gauche O/O geometry, but the ether oxygen is anti to the small C7 hydrogen rather than the methyl and the H···O contact is only about 2.34 Å, making this family less favorable. Conformers 10, 26, and 19 have staggered but doubly gauche ether-backbone geometry and anti-separated oxygens; they lack a compensating hydrogen bond. Conformer 16 has a relatively favorable short H···O contact but less ideal, approximately orthogonal backbone torsions and a more compact C3···C7 arrangement. Conformers 15, 25, and 11 have methyl-anti geometry but O-C-C-O torsions near the intermediate region, O···O about 3.11 Å, and no useful H-bond. The lower group contains increasingly compact or torsionally displaced structures. Conformer 7 retains staggered torsions but has a weakly oriented OH; 30 gains a weak H-bond but has an approximately 84-degree C3-C4-O-C6 torsion and a short C3···C7 contact. Conformers 2 and 8 have similarly nonideal first ether torsions and compact C3···C7 separations near 3.16 Å. Conformers 22 and 3 combine a folded doubly gauche backbone with O···O proximity but essentially no O-H···O stabilization. Conformers 6 and especially 4 place multiple torsions away from normal staggered minima while remaining compact; 4 additionally has the less favorable ether-anti-H arrangement. No structure shows a catastrophic atomic overlap, so separations within each geometric family are uncertain and likely small.

The cyclopropane framework has very similar C–C distances and angles in all structures, so differential ring strain is small. The main variables are rotation about the carbinol–cyclopropyl bond, rotation of the isopropyl-bearing bond, and the two O–H orientations.

The two hydroxyl oxygens divide the structures into a close/gauche set with O···O distances about 2.66–2.98 Å and an open/anti set near 3.4–3.7 Å. Most close conformers do not have a well-aligned hydrogen bond, so they retain O···O and dipolar crowding. Conformer 2 is the important exception: O···O is about 2.66 Å, H···O about 2.04 Å, and the O–H···O angle about 120°, giving the clearest, although bent, intramolecular hydrogen bond. Conformers 1 and 11 have weaker versions, with H···O near 2.14 Å and angles near 117°. Conformer 17 has H···O near 2.19 Å but a poorer angle near 112°. The remaining close forms have longer and/or more bent contacts and receive little hydrogen-bond stabilization.

Among the open O···O conformers, 23, 8, 20, 4, 12, and 28 have particularly clean heavy-atom separation and favorable staggered side-chain arrangements. For example, the isopropyl methine-to-ring hydroxyl-oxygen distances are about 3.23 Å in 23, 3.40 Å in 8, 3.15 Å in 20, and 3.24 Å in 4, while one methyl group can remain roughly anti to the ring at about 3.7–3.9 Å. Conformers 25, 6, and 22 are also open but have somewhat shorter 1,4 methine···O contacts near 2.9–3.0 Å. Conformers 30 and 5 shorten that contact to about 2.85 Å. Open conformers 29, 18, 16, and especially 7 have less favorable side-chain staggering; in 7 both methyl-to-ring separations are only roughly 3.0–3.3 Å rather than having a clearly extended methyl group.

Within the close-O···O set, 15 and 3 retain reasonable side-chain staggering and weak donor–acceptor approach, whereas 19 and 9 are sterically fairly open but lack useful O–H···O alignment. Conformers 24, 26, and 14 combine weak/bent hydroxyl contacts with less favorable torsions. Conformers 21 and 10 have additional methine···O compression around 2.86–2.89 Å. Conformer 13 is more compressed at about 2.74 Å, and conformer 27 is the clearest steric outlier at about 2.59 Å, without a compensating well-directed hydrogen bond.

No gross bond distortion or catastrophic nonbonded clash appears, so many adjacent placements—especially among 23/8/20/4/12/28 and through the middle of the list—are uncertain and could change with an electronic-structure energy calculation, dispersion treatment, or solvent. The endpoints are more defensible: 2 benefits from the best hydroxyl contact, while 27 combines the strongest 1,4 compression with poor hydroxyl alignment.

All conformers have essentially the same aziridine geometry, bond lengths, and bond angles, so differential ring strain is small. There are no classical hydrogen-bond donors; stability is therefore governed mainly by torsional strain, steric contacts, and the relative orientation of the tertiary amine and ether dipoles/lone pairs. The most favorable family keeps N and O approximately anti across N-C-C-O (N···O about 3.6-3.8 Å) and also keeps the methoxy carbon extended from the backbone (central C···OCH3 carbon about 3.6-3.7 Å). Conformers 16 and 2 best combine these features with relatively open placement of the ethyl and aziridine groups; 16 additionally has a plausible weak methyl C-H···O contact rather than a severe carbon-carbon collision. Conformer 30 retains both favorable heteroatom and methoxy torsions but has the terminal ethyl carbon near both N and the ether-bearing carbon, making it slightly more crowded. Conformers 23, 10, 26, and 22 retain the favorable long N···O separation but have a gauche C-C-O-C arrangement, placing the methoxy carbon only about 3.1 Å from the central carbon; 23 is the least crowded of this nearly degenerate group. Conformer 21 has both favorable heteroatom and methoxy orientations, but its ethyl methyl is about 3.1 Å from N and the ether-bearing CH2 approaches both aziridine carbons, reducing its advantage. Conformers 11, 13, 14, and 6 remain relatively favorable because N···O is long or nearly anti, but they incur either an ethyl-N contact, a crowded ether-aziridine orientation, or a less ideal heteroatom torsion. Conformers 15, 20, 5, 17, and 25 trade a gauche N-C-C-O arrangement (N···O near 3.0-3.1 Å) for an extended or partly extended methoxy group; 15 and 20 have the more favorable ethyl placement, whereas 5 and 25 place the ethyl methyl close to N and 17 crowds the ether-bearing CH2 against the aziridine. Conformers 7, 4, and 1 have generally acceptable ethyl/aziridine separation but both heteroatom and methoxy torsions are gauche. Conformer 29 has an extended methoxy group but combines an ethyl-N contact with a crowded ether-aziridine orientation; 9 and 8 have comparable compromises, with 8 especially compact around N and the aziridine. Conformers 18, 3, and 12 contain stronger short contacts: 18 has an ethyl methyl-N distance near 2.9 Å, while 3 and 12 have particularly short N···O distances near 2.9 Å and folded methoxy methyl-N contacts around 3.3 Å. The least favorable compact structures are 19, 27, 28, and 24. Conformer 19 folds the methoxy methyl to about 3.05 Å from N; 27 crowds the ethyl methyl simultaneously against N and the ether-bearing carbon; 28 combines an N···O gauche arrangement with an approximately 3.03 Å N···OCH3-carbon contact; and 24 has several simultaneous contacts near 3.0 Å involving the ethyl methyl, N, O, and methoxy methyl. Rankings within the middle groups are uncertain because the expected differences are small and weak C-H···O/N attractions can partly compensate steric compression.

The molecule is an acyclic, flexible diol, so there is no ring strain; the main competition is between favorable staggered/anti C–C torsions and folding that permits an intramolecular O–H···O hydrogen bond. Conformers 12, 8, 19, and 15 combine a hydrogen bond with the least strained carbon backbone. Their O···O distances are about 2.74–2.82 Å; 12 has the best overall geometry (H···O about 1.82 Å and O–H···O about 156°), followed closely by 8 and 19. The bond in 15 is more bent, about 145°, but its largely anti backbone keeps it in the leading group. Conformers 16, 3, 1, 18, 24, 13, 9, 7, 10, 23, and 17 also have clear O–H···O contacts, generally O···O about 2.73–2.87 Å, but require roughly two gauche or somewhat distorted backbone torsions. Within this group, 16 has particularly short, well-aligned geometry; 3 also has a short contact, while 1 and 18 benefit from strong primary-OH-donor to secondary-O acceptor contacts. The hydrogen bonds in 9, 10, 23, and 17 are longer, and 7 has a noticeably distorted terminal-chain torsion. Conformers 30, 22, and 27 retain strong hydrogen bonds but fold all three principal carbon-chain torsions into gauche-like arrangements, so the added torsional and steric cost lowers them. Their order is close: 30 has the most linear contact, 22 has the favorable primary-OH donor direction, and 27 is shorter but more bent. Conformer 28 has only a weak, bent contact (O···O about 2.99 Å, H···O about 2.27 Å, angle about 130°), insufficient to place it with the strongly hydrogen-bonded structures. Among the open forms, 21 and 20 have the most extended, predominantly anti skeletons; 4 is also extended but has a gauche terminal C–C–C–O arrangement. Conformer 5 has an extended carbon skeleton, but its close O···O pair is poorly oriented for hydrogen bonding and therefore introduces some lone-pair/dipolar crowding. Conformers 29, 14, 26, 11, and 2 each introduce additional gauche or distorted torsions without compensating hydrogen bonding; the central-chain gauche arrangement in 2 is relatively unfavorable. Conformers 25 and 6 are placed last because they combine folded/distorted backbones with O···O separations near 2.9 Å but O–H···O angles only around 108–115°, giving crowding with little hydrogen-bond stabilization. No severe atom-overlap is evident, so many adjacent placements—especially within the two-gauche hydrogen-bonded group and among the open conformers—are uncertain. The ranking assumes an isolated-molecule environment where intramolecular hydrogen bonding is important; polar solvent could favor the extended forms more strongly.

All structures preserve essentially the same cyclopropane geometry and normal bond lengths, so differential ring strain is small. The main discriminator is whether either ring alcohol points toward the ketone oxygen, followed by side-chain staggering and methyl–ring crowding. The strongest six-membered intramolecular O–H···O=C arrangements occur in 3 and 9 (H···O about 1.87 Å, angle about 157°) and 21 (1.91 Å, about 158°). Conformer 3 is placed just ahead of 9 because its non-hydrogen-bonded OH points more cleanly away from the side chain; this distinction is subtle. Conformers 12 and 10 retain good hydrogen bonds (about 1.95 Å and 150°), with 12 having slightly less methyl–ring crowding. Conformer 24 has a somewhat less linear but still useful contact (2.03 Å, about 141°) and a well-extended methyl orientation. Conformers 22, 18, 20, and 25 form five-membered OH···ketone contacts: 22 is best of these at roughly 1.97 Å and 138°, while 18, 20, and 25 have progressively less favorable angles near 130–132° despite good methyl–ring separation. Conformer 7 has a longer, more bent contact near 2.14 Å/127°. Conformers 4 and 27 have only weak contacts near 2.33–2.34 Å and 125–126°. Conformer 14 can make two very weak, bent approaches to the ketone and keeps the methyl group extended; 17 has an extended backbone but an inadequately directed OH near the carbonyl, making its stabilization uncertain. Among structures without a persuasive hydrogen bond, 13, 5, 8, 16, and 28 have relatively open arrangements and fewer close methyl–ring contacts; 26 is lowered because a carbonyl/alcohol oxygen approach is not accompanied by a correctly directed OH. Conformer 30 has only a long, bent contact near 2.50 Å and also a more crowded backbone. The remaining structures place the methyl carbon roughly 2.9–3.0 Å from the substituted ring region without compensating hydrogen bonding; 15 is placed last because this crowding is especially pronounced, including proximity to the tertiary alcohol. Ordering within the 14–30 region is substantially less certain than the hydrogen-bonded upper tier because the differences are mostly small torsional, dipolar, and dispersion effects that coordinates alone cannot quantify reliably.

The molecule is acyclic, so the main differences are rotations about the C–C bonds rather than ring strain. I first assessed the OH donor against both carbonyl oxygens. Conformer 19 has the best contact: H···O(ketone) is about 1.92 Å with an O–H···O angle near 138°, while its terminal groups remain well separated. Conformer 14 also has a favorable ketone contact near 2.01 Å. Conformers 28, 17, 24, and 2 have ketone-directed contacts of roughly 2.05–2.19 Å; 28 is promoted because its two carbonyls are arranged comparatively favorably, whereas 24 and especially 2 have less favorable carbonyl-dipole orientations. Conformer 8 has a relatively strong aldehyde-directed contact near 2.01 Å and good opposing carbonyl orientation, although its central C–C rotamer is more crowded than in 19, 14, or 28. Conformer 12 has a weaker but still meaningful aldehyde contact near 2.18 Å and favorable carbonyl alignment. Conformers 11, 18, 3, and 23 have progressively weaker or more bent aldehyde-directed contacts, approximately 2.18–2.24 Å with angles around 124–131°, so their hydrogen-bond stabilization is less decisive. I next compared the staggered arrangement about the bond joining the alcohol-bearing carbon to the dicarbonyl center. The least crowded pattern places the alcohol-side methyl approximately anti to the acetyl group, OH anti to the formyl group, and H anti to H; this favorable backbone pattern occurs in conformers such as 19, 14, 28, 24, 2, 4, 21, 22, 29, and 13. Alternative staggered patterns in 17, 8, 12, 11, 18, 3, and 23 put a large carbonyl substituent gauche to the methyl or OH, partly offsetting their hydrogen bonds. Among conformers without a useful OH···O contact, 4, 21, and 22 have especially favorable opposed/head-to-tail carbonyl arrangements and no conspicuous terminal clash; 29 and 13 are similarly extended but slightly less favorable. Conformers 25 and 1 retain favorable carbonyl orientations but use a less favorable central rotamer. Conformers 9, 26, and 6 are somewhat less well separated and lack hydrogen bonding. At the low-stability end, 10 and 7 place the carbonyl oxygens relatively close (about 3.5 and 3.4 Å) with unfavorable dipole alignment; 20, 27, and 16 combine a less favorable central rotamer with poor carbonyl-dipole geometry; and 15 has a favorable central stagger but a particularly unfavorable, nearly reinforcing carbonyl arrangement. No structure shows an unmistakable catastrophic atomic overlap, so ordering within the middle and lower groups is uncertain by several positions; the largest confidence is in the hydrogen-bonded, sterically favorable leaders and in the unfavorable dipole/crowding group at the end.

All structures retain essentially the same planar five-membered pyrrolic ring, so ring strain and loss of aromatic planarity are not major discriminants. The principal differences are rotations of the ethyl and hydroxymethyl substituents. First, the least crowded ethyl geometry places the terminal methyl away from both ring neighbors: its methyl-to-N and methyl-to-adjacent-C distances are typically about 3.2 and 3.5 Å. Conformers 7, 30, 29, 9, 28, 24, 19, 17, 12 and several middle-ranked structures have this favorable arrangement. A second ethyl rotamer places the methyl closer to the adjacent ring carbon, at about 3.0 Å; this modestly penalizes 5, 15, 20, 26, 4, 8, 1, 14, 16, 11 and 18. Conformer 10 is especially unfavorable because its methyl approaches N to about 2.87 Å and the N-H region to roughly 2.6 Å. Second, the best hydroxymethyl orientations keep O approximately equidistant from the two neighboring ring atoms, generally around 3.3 Å, avoiding either edge of the ring. This favors 7, 30, 29, 9, 28, 24, 20, 15 and 5; 19, 17, 12 and 26 are slightly less symmetric but remain relatively open. Rotamers with O near one ring neighbor, either N-O near 3.04 Å or O-to-adjacent-C near 2.97 Å, form the middle and lower tiers. No convincing classical intramolecular N-H...O hydrogen bond occurs: where O is close to N, the donor angle is poor. In particular, 23 and 27 have N...O distances near 2.70 Å and H...O near 2.24-2.29 Å, but N-H...O angles are only about 96 degrees, making these contacts mainly crowded rather than strongly stabilizing. Their hydroxymethyl torsions are therefore strongly penalized. Conformer 10 combines an unfavorable ethyl rotamer with a hydroxymethyl group also directed toward the N side and is placed last. Within the upper groups, especially 7/30/29/9/28/24 and 20/15/5, energy differences should be very small because they mainly reflect alcohol O-H rotation and weak dipole or dispersion effects; their detailed order is correspondingly uncertain.

The molecule is acyclic, so the main energy differences arise from torsional strain, folding of the aldehyde and propargyl arms, and intramolecular contacts rather than covalent ring strain. The clearest stabilizing feature is an O–H···O=C interaction. Conformers 30, 9, 2, 18, 26, and 4 form a six-membered hydrogen-bonded pseudoring: their H(O)···O(carbonyl) distances are approximately 1.94, 2.07, 2.08, 2.11, 2.12, and 2.14 Å, respectively. Conformer 30 is distinctly best because its contact is both shortest and least bent (about 142 degrees versus roughly 129–132 degrees for the other five). Among the remaining hydrogen-bonded structures, 9 and 2 have the strongest contacts; 9 also keeps the aldehyde and alkyne arms well separated. Conformers 18 and 26 are close, with 18 having the slightly shorter hydrogen bond and 26 the more open distal-group arrangement. Conformer 4 has the longest and most strained hydrogen bond of this set. For non-hydrogen-bonded structures, aldehyde conformations that place the carbonyl oxygen about 3.45–3.60 Å from the central carbon are favored over folded/syn arrangements. Conformers 8, 14, 29, 23, 3, 17, 21, and 7 combine this extended aldehyde geometry with a weak, geometrically constrained O–H···pi contact to the alkyne; the H-to-proximal-sp-carbon distances are about 2.4–2.5 Å. This is treated as only a small bonus because the contact is bent. Within that group, 8, 14, and 29 distribute the bulky distal groups especially well, whereas 21 is somewhat more compact and 7 places the carbonyl and alkyne carbons unusually close (about 2.8 Å). Conformers 13 and 12 are the best extended structures without the weak alkyne contact, followed by 16, 25, 28, and 24; these differences mainly reflect whether the carbonyl arm approaches the methyl or alkyne arm. Conformers 22, 1, and 20 retain an extended carbonyl but have close carbonyl/alkyne arrangements near 2.8 Å and therefore rank lower. Conformers 19, 6, and 5 have more folded aldehyde torsions, partly offset by the weak O–H···pi contact. Conformer 10 has similar folding without that compensation. Finally, 15, 11, and 27 have syn/folded aldehyde geometries, with central-C···O(carbonyl) distances near 2.95 Å; this introduces the largest torsional and nonbonded penalty, and 27 lacks even the weak alkyne contact. The ordering outside the six hydrogen-bonded conformers is uncertain at the sub-kcal/mol level because dispersion, the weak O–H···pi contacts, and carbonyl dipole effects are difficult to quantify from coordinates alone.

The dominant geometric discriminator is intramolecular O–H···O(ring) hydrogen bonding. Conformers 26, 29, 28, 24, 11, and 8 have O···O separations of about 2.77–2.82 Å and H···O separations of about 1.97–2.09 Å. Among these, 26 and 29 combine the hydrogen bond with an outward, relatively uncrowded methyl/ring arrangement. Conformer 28 has similarly low methyl crowding but a more bent hydrogen bond. Conformers 24, 11, and 8 retain the strong contact but have more compact methyl orientations; 11 also has relatively close methyl–side-chain approach, while 8 has a somewhat bent hydrogen bond. Conformer 18 has only a weak, bent contact (approximately 3.17 Å O···O and 2.58 Å H···O), so it is placed below the fully hydrogen-bonded set.

For the remaining structures, ring substitution and side-chain torsions control the estimate. A methyl group directed away from the ring interior was favored over compact pseudoaxial-like arrangements. Conformer 27 combines this favorable ring geometry with a largely extended anti/anti side chain and is therefore the best non-hydrogen-bonded structure. Conformers 21, 20, 4, 12, 6, 19, and 5 retain favorable outward methyl geometry but contain one folded/gauche side-chain relationship. Conformer 14 has a well-extended side chain but a more crowded methyl orientation, placing it below that group.

Conformers 22, 17, 13, 2, and 16 have favorable methyl orientation but more compact, approximately gauche/gauche side chains; they are penalized for torsional strain and less favorable dipole/steric organization. Conformers 15, 9, 23, 10, 30, 7, and 25 have compact methyl arrangements plus one folded side-chain torsion, with 15, 9, and 23 judged least crowded within that set. Conformers 1 and 3 combine compact methyl geometry with compact gauche/gauche side chains and no compensating hydrogen bond, making them the least favorable estimates. No structure shows an unmistakable catastrophic nonbonded clash, so ordering within each torsional/ring-geometry tier is uncertain and could change with a quantitative force-field or electronic-structure calculation.

Step 1: The principal stabilizing fold is a six-membered N···C=O donor–acceptor arrangement involving the imine nitrogen lone pair and the aldehyde carbon. Conformers 6, 30, 20, and 29 have very short N···C(carbonyl) separations of about 2.1 Å and N–C–O approach angles near 100–105°, close to a Bürgi–Dunitz trajectory. I interpret this repeated, directional geometry as a strong n(N)→pi*(C=O)/electrostatic interaction rather than an accidental N/O clash. Among these, 6 and 30 also place the carbonyl oxygen approximately eclipsing the small alpha C–H bond; 6 has the more favorable extended ether-side arrangement, followed by 30. Conformers 20 and 29 retain the strong N···C interaction but have less favorable aldehyde/side-chain torsions, with 29 the more distorted and crowded of the pair. Step 2: Conformers 21, 2, and 1 show the same approximately tetrahedral approach to the carbonyl carbon at longer N···C distances, roughly 2.8–3.0 Å, so they receive a smaller donor–acceptor stabilization. Of these, 21 has the shortest and best-defined contact, followed by 2 and 1. Step 3: No conformer has a convincing conventional N–H···O(carbonyl) hydrogen bond. Even where H···O is around 2.8–3.2 Å, the N–H vector points largely away from the oxygen, so those contacts were not treated as hydrogen bonds. Step 4: Outside the folded N···C set, favorable aldehyde torsion is indicated by an O(carbonyl)···H(alpha) separation near 2.55–2.63 Å, corresponding to the carbonyl oxygen eclipsing the least bulky alpha substituent. Conformers 15, 24, 7, 26, 9, 17, 18, and 11 benefit from this geometry. Conformers 15 and 24 additionally keep the carbonyl and ether oxygens widely separated, about 4.6–4.7 Å, and avoid terminal crowding. Conformer 7 is more extended but has a somewhat closer O···O arrangement; 26 and 9 are extended at the terminal C–O bond but place the ether oxygen gauche to both carbon substituents. Conformers 17, 18, and 11 are progressively less favorable because of additional gauche folding or closer heteroatom contacts. Step 5: Conformers 28, 16, and 4 have no special N···C interaction but are relatively open and staggered. Conformer 28 has especially good carbonyl/ether separation, whereas 16 and 4 benefit from an extended terminal ether–imine torsion. Conformer 8 is also extended but has the carbonyl oxygen oriented toward the bulkier CH2O substituent, lowering it relative to those methyl-oriented structures. Step 6: Conformers 27, 3, and 19 are ordinary gauche rotamers with no severe contact; 27 and 3 are slightly more extended than 19. Conformers 13 and 10 have an extended terminal group but place the ether oxygen gauche to both alpha-carbon substituents and have relatively close O···O separations. Step 7: Conformers 12, 14, and 22 avoid major clashes but use the less favorable aldehyde orientation toward the CH2O side; 12 and 14 keep the heteroatoms somewhat farther apart than 22. Conformers 25 and 23 combine multiple gauche relationships with O···O distances near 3.6–3.7 Å. Conformer 5 is placed last because it combines the aldehyde orientation toward the bulky CH2O branch with the shortest carbonyl-O···ether-O contact, about 3.16 Å, and lacks a compensating N···C or hydrogen-bond interaction. The middle of the ranking is intrinsically uncertain because several structures differ only by weak gauche, dipolar, and dispersion effects; the largest interpretive uncertainty is whether the exceptionally short N···C contacts are treated as stabilizing donor–acceptor folds or as excessive compression, although their repeated near-Bürgi–Dunitz geometry supports the former interpretation.

All six-membered rings are chair-like: the three opposite-carbon distances are generally about 2.75–3.00 Å, with no clear boat, twist-boat, or strongly eclipsed ring. The methyl and hydroxymethyl bonds also point predominantly outward from their local ring-carbon environments, so the ranking is not controlled by a large axial-substituent penalty. The main distinction is therefore hydroxymethyl orientation. The less crowded C–C rotamers place O about 2.9–3.1 Å from one adjacent ring carbon and about 3.7–3.8 Å from the other; examples include 3, 6, 14, 17, 20, 22, 24 and 26. A more crowded family places O near both adjacent ring carbons, as in 2, 8, 11, 16, 25, 27, 29 and 30. Rotation about C–O provides a second discriminator. Conformers 14, 17, 20, 21, 25 and 26 have the O–H bond directed relatively outward, with the hydroxyl H roughly 3.2 Å from the substituted ring carbon, minimizing inward O–H/C–H contacts; 15 has a similar favorable hydroxyl orientation but a somewhat closer approach to the methyl side. Thus 17, 14 and 20 lead the rotamer that is directed away from the methyl-bearing side, followed by the analogous 26 and 21 geometries. Among inward/gauche hydroxyl rotamers, 6, 3, 24, 18, 22, 5 and 10 retain comparatively clean heavy-atom separation. Conformers 13, 28, 19, 4, 7, 23 and 1 have progressively less favorable secondary H contacts or methyl-side crowding. Conformer 25 is the best member of the two-sided O-contact family because its O–H bond points outward. At the unstable end, 11 has a moderate O/methyl approach, 30 and 8 combine two-sided O crowding with short inward hydroxyl-H contacts, and 9 has both an approximately 2.82 Å O-to-ring-carbon contact and an approximately 3.4 Å O-to-methyl-carbon approach. Conformer 12 is placed last because O approaches the methyl carbon at about 3.10 Å and one methyl H at roughly 2.2 Å, the clearest steric conflict in the set. Differences within the leading and middle groups are subtle and likely only a few tenths of a kcal/mol; without an explicit force field or electronic energies, the exact ordering inside those groups is uncertain.

All conformers have normal covalent geometry, so the main discriminator is intramolecular hydrogen bonding followed by the torsional cost required to make that contact. The strongest motif is alcohol O–H···O=C(formamide). Conformers 1, 2, 3, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16, and 20 contain this contact. Conformers 1 and 16 combine a nearly linear contact with relatively favorable, largely anti backbone arrangements: for 1, H···O is about 1.92 Å, and for 16 it is about 1.99 Å with an almost linear angle. Conformers 3 and 9 also have short, well-directed contacts near 1.92 Å. Conformer 13 has the shortest contact, about 1.87 Å, but its central backbone is more torsionally distorted, reducing the net benefit. Conformer 2 has a short but less linear contact; 20 has a very linear but slightly longer contact and an additional gauche carbon–carbon interaction. Conformer 15 is somewhat more bent, while 11 and especially 10 have longer, more bent O–H···O=C contacts near 2.1 Å.

A second stabilizing family uses N–H···O(alcohol). Conformers 18 and 6 have the best versions, with H···O distances near 1.91–1.93 Å and angles around 143–147 degrees. Conformers 14 and 19 are also clearly hydrogen bonded; 19 has the shorter contact but requires a more crowded arrangement in which both carbon substituents are gauche to the downstream chain. Conformer 28 has the same contact but similar extra crowding and a longer H···O distance. Conformers 8 and 7 have only weak, bent N–H···O contacts, approximately 2.17 Å with angles near 130 degrees.

Among conformers without a convincing internal hydrogen bond, 26 is favored by its relatively anti central backbone and absence of a close heteroatom clash. Conformers 23, 17, 5, 24, 30, 12, and 21 are mostly open, staggered structures with the hydroxymethyl branch approximately anti to the downstream chain; their differences are small and mainly reflect terminal dipole orientation and modest gauche interactions. Conformers 29 and 25 retain more compact or less favorable branch arrangements. Conformers 4 and 22 bring heteroatoms relatively close without correctly orienting either donor hydrogen, giving little hydrogen-bond compensation. Conformer 27 places both carbon substituents gauche to the downstream chain and has no useful donor–acceptor alignment, making it the least favorable estimate. Ordering within the weakly interacting open group, and between the weakest O–H···O=C and strongest N–H···O conformers, is the most uncertain part of the ranking.

1. The three-membered C–C–N ring has essentially the same geometry in all structures, so differential ring strain is small; the ranking is controlled mainly by side-chain torsions and intramolecular hydrogen bonding. 2. Conformer 1 has the clearest alcohol-to-amine hydrogen bond: O···N is about 2.72 Å, H···N about 2.13 Å, and the O–H···N angle about 151°. Although this requires a folded backbone with additional gauche contacts, the amine is a stronger acceptor than an alcohol oxygen, making 1 the best candidate. 3. Conformers 30, 22, 29, 24, 21, 3, 11, and 14 combine a vicinal O–H···O contact with the least crowded principal backbone arrangement. Their CH2OH and aziridine substituents are approximately anti across the central C–C bond, as indicated by terminal C···C separations near 3.88 Å. Conformer 30 has the best O–H···O geometry in this set, with H···O about 1.92 Å and O···O about 2.70 Å. The corresponding contacts in 22, 29, 24, and 21 remain favorable, while those in 3, 11, and especially 14 are progressively longer or more bent. 4. Conformers 5, 20, 26, 16, and 9 also have short O–H···O contacts, generally H···O around 1.95–2.01 Å, but the aziridine substituent is no longer anti to the CH2OH group. Their hydrogen bonds compensate much, but probably not all, of the added gauche crowding. 5. Conformers 28, 25, and 18 retain a comparatively favorable anti backbone but lack a well-oriented internal hydrogen bond. Conformer 28 has a weak residual O–H···O approach, whereas 25 is more fully extended. Conformer 18 has a short O···N approach without useful donor alignment, which may instead introduce lone-pair/steric repulsion. 6. Conformers 7, 23, 12, 4, 8, and 13 have increasingly bent O–H···O contacts while also retaining the less favorable crowded backbone. Conformer 13 has the weakest geometry of this hydrogen-bonded subgroup. 7. Conformers 2, 27, 6, 10, 15, and 19 have neither a good internal hydrogen bond nor the best large-group anti arrangement; they are ranked mainly by smaller differences in oxygen separation, dipole orientation, and nonbonded crowding. Conformer 17 is placed last because it combines the crowded backbone with widely separated heteroatoms and no compensating hydrogen bond. The ordering within the middle groups, especially 5–18 and 2–19, is uncertain at roughly the level expected for subtle torsional and dispersion effects not reliably recoverable from geometry alone.

1. All structures have essentially the same local bond geometry and are acyclic, so the main differences are intramolecular hydrogen bonding and the anti/gauche pattern of the O–(CH2)4–OH chain. No conformer shows a grossly distorted bond or catastrophic nonbonded overlap. 2. Conformers 18, 27, 22, and 29 form the clearest terminal O–H···O(ether) hydrogen bonds. Their H···O distances are approximately 1.87, 1.90, 1.91, and 2.01 Å, respectively, with O–H···O angles around 159°, 154°, 153°, and 155°. Conformer 18 combines the shortest, most linear contact with a relatively favorable anti first chain torsion; 27 is similar but slightly less optimal. Conformers 22 and 29 require more all-gauche folding, and 29 has the longest hydrogen bond, placing them next. 3. Conformers 3 and 4 also close into O–H···O pseudorings, but the contacts are weaker and bent: about 2.07 Å/139° for 3 and 2.22 Å/138° for 4. Conformer 3 is favored over 4 because it retains one anti chain torsion and has the shorter contact. 4. Conformer 1 is the best non-hydrogen-bonded extended geometry: three of the four principal chain torsions are anti, minimizing gauche and syn-pentane interactions. It is placed close to 3 because the energetic advantage of 3's bent hydrogen bond over 1's lower torsional strain is uncertain. 5. Conformers 19, 25, 9, 5, 26, and 2 each have two anti and two gauche chain torsions without a serious close-contact sequence. They should form a nearly degenerate low-energy nonbonded tier; the listed order reflects small differences in end-to-end separation, oxygen–oxygen dipole separation, and terminal-OH exposure rather than a robust energetic distinction. 6. Conformer 21 also has two anti torsions, but its final gauche/gauche sequence brings C6 and the terminal oxygen to roughly 3.0 Å, introducing a syn-pentane-like penalty. Conformer 6 has more torsional folding but gains a weak N–H···O(terminal) contact (H···O about 2.45 Å, angle about 128°), so it follows closely. 7. Conformers 20, 24, 16, 23, 11, and 30 generally retain one anti torsion and lack a strong hydrogen bond. Their ordering is consequently uncertain; 24 and 16 have favorably directed but too-long N–H···O approaches, while 23, 11, and 30 are mainly distinguished by weak steric and dipolar effects. 8. Conformers 17 and 14 are all-gauche helices, but their gauche rotations have mostly the same sense and avoid the worst 1,5 contacts. Conformers 28, 15, 13, and 7 each contain only one anti torsion plus at least one unfavorable opposite-gauche or compact contact, with no compensating short hydrogen bond. 9. Conformers 8, 12, and 10 are the least favorable: they are essentially all-gauche and contain an unfavorable compact gauche/gauche segment. In 10 the ether and terminal oxygens approach to about 3.35 Å, but the hydroxyl hydrogen is poorly oriented for bonding, so the fold gives oxygen–oxygen proximity without useful hydrogen-bond compensation. The middle of the ranking, especially the two-anti and one-anti tiers, is substantially less certain than the hydrogen-bonded top and compact bottom tiers.

The connectivity is N≡C–CH2–O–CH2–CH2–cyclopropyl. All cyclopropane rings have similar bond lengths and angles, so differential ring strain is small; the ranking is controlled mainly by the C–C–O–C, C–O–C–C, and O–C–C–cyclopropyl torsions. For the cyano-adjacent C–C–O–C torsion, I favor a staggered gauche geometry because it can benefit from the cyano-substituted ether/anomeric interaction; for the other two backbone torsions, staggered anti arrangements generally minimize steric and eclipsing strain. Thus conformers 13 and 21, which combine cyano-side gauche with anti geometries for both downstream torsions, form the best pair. Conformers 14 and 29 retain the favorable cyano-side gauche geometry and only one ordinary ether-side gauche torsion. Conformers 7 and 10 are fully extended and staggered but lose some cyano-side gauche stabilization; they remain very competitive and are nearly degenerate. Conformers 5 and 30 have one downstream gauche torsion and modest displacement of the cyano-side torsion from its ideal staggered value. Conformers 9, 4, 6, 8, and 27 instead place the O–CH2–CH2–cyclopropyl segment gauche; 9 and 4 are the least folded members of this group. Conformer 20 has otherwise favorable backbone geometry but places the chain approximately anti to the cyclopropyl methine H, creating two less favorable chain/ring gauche relationships. Conformers 28, 25, and 15 have cyano-side anti plus one downstream gauche torsion, while 24 has cyano-side anti and a gauche O–CH2–CH2–cyclopropyl torsion. Conformers 17, 2, 22, and 3 are well-staggered all-gauche backbones: they avoid eclipsing but accumulate two ordinary gauche penalties; 17/2 and 22/3 are close near-degenerate pairs. Conformer 18 is also all-gauche but somewhat displaced from the preferred cyano-side torsion. Conformer 19 is locally staggered but combines cyano-side anti with both downstream gauche arrangements. The lowest group contains geometries forced substantially away from staggered minima: 16 has a distorted ether-side gauche torsion; 26 additionally has the unfavorable cyclopropyl orientation; 23 has both downstream torsions displaced toward partially eclipsed values. In 12 the C–O–C–C torsion is near roughly 100 degrees rather than a staggered minimum, and in 1 the O–C–C–cyclopropyl torsion is similarly near 100 degrees. Conformer 11 combines large distortions in both the cyano-side and terminal backbone torsions and is therefore placed last. There are no classical hydrogen-bond donors; folded C–H···N/O contacts are weak and do not outweigh the torsional ordering. Uncertainty is greatest among the near-degenerate pairs and among conformers 5–10 and 14–30, where gauche-effect, dispersion, and steric contributions are comparable.

The molecule contains a conformationally flexible seven-membered unsaturated ether ring and an allylic CH2OH substituent. First, no conformer has a convincing intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bond: the hydroxyl and ring-ether oxygens are generally about 3.5-5 Å apart, and the few shorter H...O approaches have poor directionality. Ring strain therefore dominates. The least strained ring-pucker family is 28/14/3/9/20/7/27/22/21: opposite-ring heavy-atom separations are mostly near 3.1-3.2 Å and representative single-bond torsions are approximately 60-80 degrees, avoiding major eclipsing. The next family is 10/1/13/25/2/17/23/18; it has two moderately compressed or partly eclipsed torsions near 35-40 degrees and several approximately 2.8-2.9 Å transannular approaches. The 30/29/26/24/12/15/6/19 family is less favorable because it contains stronger approximately 14-25 degree eclipsing distortions and a recurrent approximately 2.70 Å opposite-ring approach. The 16/4/8/5/11 family is least favorable: it combines a nearly eclipsed approximately 14 degree torsion with additional roughly 35-46 degree torsions. Within each ring family, the allylic CH2OH rotamer breaks the ties. Skew O-C-C=C arrangements around 110-130 degrees with the hydroxyl hydrogen directed outward are preferred; syn/eclipsed rotamers with hydroxyl O...alkenyl-C contacts around 2.73-2.82 Å are penalized. Thus 28 and 14 lead the low-strain family, while 27, 22, and especially 21 are lower within it. Similar criteria place 10, 1, and 13 ahead of the syn-oriented 17, 23, and 18 in the second family. Differences between immediate neighbors are uncertain because no electronic energies are supplied; the closest calls are 28/14, 3/9, 27/22, 10/1/13, and 30/29/26/24.

The bicyclic ether framework has essentially the same puckering and bond geometry throughout, so differential ring strain is small; the ranking is governed mainly by the hydroxyethyl torsions. Conformers 14 and 9 are the only clear intramolecular O–H···O(ether) structures. Conformer 14 has the better geometry (H···O about 2.00 Å and O–H···O about 164°), while 9 is slightly longer and more bent (about 2.05 Å and 153°), placing 14 first. Among the non-hydrogen-bonded structures, 8, 25, 17, 5, 16, 13, 26, 10, and 4 have the most extended terminal O–C–C–C arrangements, with alcohol-O to substituted-ring-C separations near 3.7–3.8 Å; these generally minimize gauche and core contacts. Within that set, 8/25 place the terminal chain on the less crowded side of the bicyclic framework, 17/5/16 are slightly closer to a bridgehead region, and 26/10/4 show closer approximately 3.0 Å side-chain/core approaches. Conformer 18 is a relatively unstrained skew/near-extended case and is placed between the cleaner extended and compact gauche families. Conformers 28, 7, 12, and 1 retain favorable outward-pointing O–H orientations but have a gauche hydroxyethyl backbone. The following structures increasingly fold the alcohol toward ring carbons without forming an O–H···O bond; 23, 29, 6, and 30 are somewhat less crowded than 19, 20, 2, and 27. Conformers 22, 15, 3, and 11 combine compact torsions with less favorable side-chain/core proximity or dipole placement. Conformers 21 and especially 24 have the strongest unsupported folding; in 24 the alcohol oxygen approaches a ring carbon to roughly 2.7 Å while its hydrogen points away from the ether oxygen, giving crowding without compensating hydrogen bonding. Ordering inside the broad non-hydrogen-bonded tiers is uncertain because many differences are only alcohol-rotor or weak C–H···O/contact effects, and no electronic energies are available.

The dominant geometric discriminator is intramolecular O–H···O hydrogen bonding. Conformers 8 and 3 have the best contacts: O···O distances are about 2.88 and 2.87 Å, H···O distances about 1.92 and 1.91 Å, and donor–H···acceptor angles near 170°, so they receive the largest stabilization. Conformer 14 also has a strong contact (O···O about 2.89 Å, H···O about 1.94 Å, angle about 165°), followed by 4, whose approximately 2.92 Å O···O and 1.99 Å H···O contact is less linear, near 160°. None of the other conformers has a comparably credible hydrogen bond. The cyclobutane rings otherwise have normal bond lengths and comparable butterfly puckering, with no clear catastrophic ring distortion, so ring-strain differences appear secondary. Among the non-hydrogen-bonded structures, conformers 27, 22, 11, 6, 30, 12, and 24 have the most extended O–C–C–C side-chain geometry: the terminal O lies roughly 3.7–3.8 Å from the substituted ring carbon, reducing gauche and over-ring contacts. Conformer 27 combines this with both hydroxyl hydrogens directed relatively outward; 22 has a favorable terminal O–H rotamer, while 11 and 6 have an outward-facing ring hydroxyl. Conformers 30 and 12 remain extended but have somewhat less favorable hydroxyl rotamers. In 24 the carbon chain lies closer over the ring framework, making it the least favorable member of this extended group. Conformers 25 and 15 are the best of the gauche-backbone group because their two oxygens remain widely separated (about 6.2 Å), both hydroxyl orientations avoid the ring, and the terminal O–H geometry is relatively unencumbered. Conformer 16 is similarly open, whereas 7 brings the hydroxyl regions somewhat closer and has a less favorable inward ring-OH orientation. Conformers 19, 26, 10, 21, 28, 1, and 18 have ordinary nonbonded gauche side chains without severe clashes; their ordering mainly reflects how far the terminal oxygen stays from the ring and whether the ring O–H points outward. Conformer 5 is more folded, with an O···O separation around 4.26 Å, but the hydrogens do not point so as to form a hydrogen bond. Conformers 9, 13, 2, 17, and 20 likewise lack hydrogen bonding and have less favorable combinations of gauche backbone and inward hydroxyl orientation. Conformers 29 and 23 are folded enough to bring the oxygens to about 3.85 and 4.05 Å, respectively, yet both O–H bonds point away from the other oxygen; thus they pay folding and dipolar/steric costs without hydrogen-bond compensation. Beyond the first four structures, the expected energy differences are small and the detailed order is correspondingly uncertain because hydroxyl torsional energies, weak dispersion, and subtle cyclobutane puckering cannot be quantified reliably from geometry alone.

The common connectivity is an aldehyde–(CH2)2–C≡C–aziridine chain. The carbonyl and aziridine geometries, including three-membered-ring bond lengths, are very similar throughout, so differential ring strain is small. No conformer has a convincing intramolecular N–H···O hydrogen bond: even the most folded structures have H(N)···O separations around 3.6–3.9 Å with poor orientation. The main energetic discriminator is therefore the two saturated-chain torsions. Using O···second-CH2 and carbonyl-C···first-sp-C separations to identify anti versus gauche arrangements gives an anti/anti set {12,19,24,25,29}, an anti/gauche set {1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,11,15,16,18,20,21,22,23,26,27,28,30}, a gauche/anti set {7,14,17}, and a gauche/gauche set {9,13}. Anti/anti structures should be lowest because they avoid both the carbonyl/beta-carbon and CHO/ethynyl gauche contacts. Within that nearly degenerate set, 24 and 12 are the most open and show the least possibility of remote crowding; 29, 19, and 25 follow very closely. The anti/gauche conformers retain the favorable aldehyde torsion but pay one ordinary chain-gauche penalty. Conformers 21 and 15 keep the carbonyl oxygen especially far from the nearby sp carbon, followed by the relatively open 27, 8, 20, 23, 5, 6, 11, and 10 geometries. More folded members remain close in energy because their terminal groups are still too far apart for strong interactions. Conformers 18, 4, and 16 orient the carbonyl oxygen somewhat more toward the alkyne, while 28 has the shortest nonbonded carbonyl-C···sp-C separation in this class and the most compact O/N arrangement, so these are placed toward the bottom of the one-gauche tier. The gauche/anti structures have a short O···beta-carbon geometry near 2.82 Å; 17 additionally places a beta C–H unusually close to O, making it the least favorable of that subgroup. Finally, 13 and 9 contain both gauche torsions. Conformer 9 is ranked last because its approximately 2.75 Å O···sp-carbon approach is the clearest additional nonbonded compression. Rotations of the aziridine around the nearly cylindrically symmetric alkyne axis contribute only small differences, so ordering within each torsional tier—especially the first five and the broad anti/gauche group—is uncertain by likely only a few tenths of a kcal/mol.

The oxetane ring geometry and bond lengths are broadly similar throughout, so the main discriminants are side-chain torsions and intramolecular O–H···O contacts. First, conformers 22, 13, and 5 have the only convincing hydroxyl-to-aldehyde hydrogen bonds. For 22, H···O(carbonyl) is about 1.92 Å with an O···O distance of 2.86 Å and an almost linear angle near 164°, making it the clearest minimum. Conformer 5 has approximately 1.94/2.83 Å and 152°, but its carbonyl oxygen is in a more folded, sterically less favorable orientation relative to the ring attachment. Conformer 13 has a slightly longer contact, about 2.04/2.90 Å and 146°, but a more extended aldehyde-side-chain geometry; this places it between 22 and 5 overall. Second, 14, 25, 8, 3, and 4 combine relatively extended aldehyde orientations with short hydroxyl-to-ring-oxygen contacts. These contacts are geometrically bent, generally near 110°, so they are weaker than the carbonyl hydrogen bonds, but they still provide modest stabilization; 14 has the shortest H···O(ring) separation, about 2.15 Å, while the others are around 2.23–2.26 Å. Conformer 21 also has a short ring-oxygen contact, but the hydroxyl oxygen lies only about 2.93 Å from the carbonyl oxygen without directing its proton there, introducing acceptor–acceptor crowding. Third, 29, 17, 12, 28, and 27 retain extended aldehyde chains and weaker hydroxyl/ring-oxygen approaches of roughly 2.56–2.66 Å; they should be close in energy. Conformers 20, 30, 2, 9, and 1 are largely open structures with no useful hydrogen bond but also little severe crowding, so they follow the weakly stabilized extended forms. Conformer 11 has a less extended carbonyl torsion and only a weak ring-oxygen contact. Conformers 15 and 7 gain short hydroxyl/ring-oxygen contacts but use folded, syn-like aldehyde orientations, reducing the benefit. Conformer 6 additionally places the hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygens about 2.84 Å apart without a properly directed proton. Conformer 24 has an extended side chain but a similarly unproductive approximately 2.91 Å O···O approach. Conformer 18 lacks compensating hydrogen bonding and has a less favorable intermediate carbonyl torsion. The least favorable group, 10, 19, 26, 16, and especially 23, has folded carbonyl orientations with little or no effective hydrogen bonding; 23 also combines this with an unproductive approximately 2.92 Å hydroxyl-oxygen/carbonyl-oxygen contact. There are no obvious catastrophic clashes, so ordering within the middle and lower tiers is uncertain and likely corresponds to sub-kcal/mol differences.

Step 1: The epoxide bond lengths and local three-membered-ring geometries are essentially unchanged across the set, so differential ring strain is small; the ranking is controlled mainly by rotations about the central C–C and C–N bonds, intramolecular hydrogen bonding, and nonbonded crowding. Step 2: Conformers 4 and 30 contain the clearest six-membered OH···O=C contacts. Their H···O distances are about 1.84 and 1.86 Å, respectively, with O–H···O angles near 153 degrees. Conformer 4 is preferred because the amide N and epoxide-bearing side are more nearly anti and better separated (N···C2 about 3.75 Å versus about 2.8 Å in 30), while retaining the same strong hydrogen bond. Step 3: Conformers 22 and 29 have weaker folded OH···O=C contacts: H···O is about 2.26–2.29 Å and the angles are only about 129–132 degrees. They are nevertheless favored over most open structures, with 22 having the slightly better contact and less crowding. Step 4: Conformers 19, 16, and 18 combine relatively favorable extended/anti backbone arrangements with short but geometrically constrained OH···epoxide-O approaches. These contacts are weaker than the carbonyl hydrogen bonds because their angles are only roughly 115–121 degrees; 19 has especially good separation of the amide-bearing and epoxide portions, while 16 has the shortest such H···O distance, about 2.00 Å. Step 5: Conformers 2, 8, and 27 are open, well-staggered structures without a significant internal hydrogen bond. Their low steric congestion makes them competitive with the weakly hydrogen-bonded structures. Step 6: Conformers 15, 28, and 17 have constrained N–H···epoxide-O interactions, with H···O distances around 2.20–2.27 Å and angles around 121–127 degrees. These provide some stabilization, but require a less favorable gauche backbone; 15 has the best geometry of the three. Step 7: Conformers 1, 5, 25, 10, and 23 retain a favorable amide-versus-epoxide anti relationship but place the central carbon substituent gauche to both atoms of the epoxide more closely, without a compensating hydrogen bond. Step 8: Conformers 6, 14, and 13 have acceptable epoxide-side staggering but a less favorable central amide rotamer. Conformers 3 and 12 obtain only weak, bent OH···epoxide contacts and remain slightly less favorable. Step 9: The final group has the amide N gauche to both the alcohol and epoxide-bearing substituents or otherwise has compact nonbonded geometry. Conformer 20 is helped by a weak OH···epoxide contact; 26 and 24 have comparatively good separation of the epoxide carbon from the side chain. Conformers 9, 7, and 11 lack a useful donor–acceptor contact, and 21 is the most compact, with the side-chain carbon simultaneously close to both epoxide atoms and no compensating hydrogen bond. The middle and lower portions are uncertain because many differences are ordinary gauche/anti and dipolar effects likely below a few kilocalories per mole; labels adjacent in those regions should be regarded as near-ties.

All structures retain essentially the same two cyclopropane geometries, so differential ring strain is small; no conformer shows a clearly broken bond or exceptional ring deformation. There is only one oxygen, an alcohol, so no conventional intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bond is possible. The largest discriminator is the C3-C7-C9-C10 backbone torsion. Conformers 3, 7, 8, 12, 13, 17, 20, 21, 23, 25, 27, and 28 have extended, anti-like backbones, with C3...C10 near 3.85 A. The others are gauche-like, with C3...C10 about 3.00-3.16 A, and therefore incur additional 1,4 carbon-carbon and cross-ring steric interactions. Within each backbone class, rotation at the first cyclopropyl-chain junction matters: placing C9 approximately anti to the oxygen-bearing ring carbon C2 is preferable to placing it anti to C4, because the latter brings C9 closer to the C2-O side of the first ring. Alcohol rotation gives three approximate families. O-H anti to the substituted C2-C3 direction, identified by H(O)...C3 near 3.2 A, is taken as best; O-H anti toward the other ring bond is next; the orientation with H(O) directed more toward the chain, H(O)...C3 near 2.6 A and H(O)...C7 commonly near 2.7 A, is slightly less favorable. These alcohol effects are weaker than the central anti/gauche distinction. Among the anti structures this favors 20 and 13, followed by 25 and 3; 23 and 8 retain the favorable first junction but have the less favorable O-H direction. Structures 12 and 28, then 17 and 21, and finally 7 and 27 use the less favorable first-junction orientation. In the gauche set, 30 and 18 combine the best alcohol and first-junction arrangements. Conformers 11, 14, and 19 have the favorable first junction and the intermediate O-H rotamer; 19 is placed lower because an additional cross-ring C...C approach is near 3.3 A. Conformers 22, 26, 9, and 15 retain the favorable junction but point O-H more toward the chain; 9 and 15 also have closer secondary ring-ring contacts. Conformers 6 and especially 16 use the less favorable junction, with 16 having the most compressed C3...C10 separation, about 2.99 A. Conformers 10 and 2 have the same junction disadvantage plus less favorable compact packing; 2 is appreciably torsionally displaced and has a roughly 3.4 A cross-ring carbon contact. The final group, 24, 1, 29, 4, and 5, combines a gauche backbone, the less favorable first-junction orientation, and the chain-directed O-H rotamer; 5 also shows both distorted compact geometry and a close cross-ring contact. Exact ordering within paired anti conformers and within the compact gauche subgroups is uncertain because their geometries differ only by small terminal cyclopropyl rotations and dispersion contacts. The boundary between the least favorable anti structures and the best gauche structures is also relatively uncertain, but the anti-first ordering follows the dominant torsional and steric trend.

The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, so classical intramolecular hydrogen bonding cannot distinguish the conformers. The main factors are therefore torsional strain in the large carbocyclic perimeter, transannular crowding, the orientation of the acetate carbonyl, and smaller carbonyl/ether dipole effects. The epoxide and unsaturated lactone geometries are broadly conserved, so their intrinsic bond strain is nearly constant.
